description: Claude, map mars, make no mistakes.
summary:
On Mars, an astronaut on a spacewalk cannot ask Earth for help: a message takes up to 24 minutes each way. There is no GPS, no compass (Mars has no global magnetic field) and no signs. AREO helps make that walk's key decision before leaving: can I go and come back safely, and by which way?

The astronaut marks the habitat and the destination, like in Google Maps, and picks a departure time. A 4D planner finds the safest route, not the shortest, over 1 m HiRISE terrain of Jezero and Gale craters: slope, shadows at the time each spot is reached, radio contact with the habitat, oxygen, battery and radiation. It gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict that names what limits the walk, and guides the astronaut with landmarks and the Sun, without GPS.

A training mode turns the same planner into guided missions where students learn why the shortest route is not always the safest, checked against the planner's real answers.

Every number shows where it comes from. Missing data is shown as missing, never invented. Educational prototype, not flight software.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AREO answers the questions of someone standing on Mars with a helmet on and little time:

- Can I step here? Slope and terrain hazard at 1 m: slope, roughness, and probable loose soil from THEMIS night infrared. Above 25° the terrain counts as impassable, both on the map and in the planner.

- Which way do I go, and how do I get back? A 4D (space + time) planner: an A* search over the 1 m elevation model whose cost combines slope, shadow at the time each cell is reached, and loss of radio line of sight to the habitat. The return trip is included by default.

- Will my oxygen and battery last? Suit consumption leg by leg with the Pandolf metabolic model adapted to Mars gravity (0.38 g), including the tools the astronaut carries (masses of real Apollo tools).

- How much radiation will I get? A dose budget for the walk, based on the surface dose measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument and scaled by how much sky is visible along the route.

- How much daylight is left? Hour-by-hour shadow maps computed from the terrain and NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, including the crater rim up to 100 km away, with a Sun slider on the map.

- Can the habitat hear me? Where there is radio line of sight to the habitat, and the longest stretch of the route without it.

- Where do I take cover? Shelters (spots with little visible sky) and walking minutes to the nearest one.

- How do I navigate without GPS? Step-by-step directions based on what can be seen from 1.7 m eye height ("head toward the hill at 12 o'clock, about 8 min"), using named features, craters and hills, plus the Sun and your own shadow to confirm the heading. Vikings crossed oceans with the sky; astronauts can cross Jezero with the Sun.

The verdict uses hard limits that do not compensate each other (slope, O2 and battery reserve, back before sunset, minutes without contact, radiation dose). It names the limiting factor and re-tests the route in stress scenarios (leaving 30 min late, walking 20% slower, carrying 10% more), saying in how many it still holds. There is also a first-person view of the horizon from each stop, rendered over the real terrain.

TRAINING MODE

The same planner becomes a set of guided missions for students and the general public, built like an onboarding: a floating card points at the part of the screen it talks about, with one short sentence per step and an optional "go deeper" section with the numbers. Each mission teaches one difficulty of a real EVA:

- Don't trust a number without a source (provenance badges).

- You can't walk anywhere (slope forces detours).

- The map changes with the time of day (the 4D part: same points, different departure time, different verdict).

- Air and battery run out.

- Losing sight of the habitat means losing the radio.

- Radiation adds up.

- Plans fail (predict what will limit the route, then make it hold in stress scenarios).

- What we don't know (what the model cannot evaluate yet).

- Final mission: pick a real destination, predict, and make the route GO and robust, then print it.

The key rule: a lesson has no numbers of its own. Every number it shows and every answer it checks comes from the planner's real response, so if a safety limit changes, the lessons update by themselves. When the server lacks the data to complete a task, the lesson says so and lets you skip it, but never marks it as done or fakes the result. There are no speed or distance rankings: in a safety planner, that would reward risky plans. The design follows research on educational games: learning gains come from step-by-step support and repeated play, not from story or visual realism.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline downloads NASA data politely (one request at a time per server, honoring the PDS crawl delay) and precomputes every heavy layer: slope, hazard, hourly shadows, visible sky, shelters and places. A FastAPI backend only reads those outputs and answers point queries and route requests. A React + MapLibre GL + Three.js frontend draws the map, the 3D terrain and the horizon view. It runs on a small AWS EC2 server with nginx, and every change merged to main is deployed automatically. The interface is available in Spanish and English.

WHY IT MATTERS

A crewed mission to Mars is decades of work and billions of dollars, and at the center of it is a person walking with a fixed supply of oxygen and power. Existing maps show layers of data, but they do not answer the question that matters on the ground: can I go and come back with margin? AREO turns NASA data into that decision. It is also a teaching tool: the training mode lets a student plan their own walk with real NASA data and discover, mission by mission, why the shortest route is not always the safest.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

- Safest route, not shortest: the planner trades distance for risk, and the time of day changes the answer.

- Honesty about data: every number carries a badge (OBSERVED, DERIVED, MODELED or ASSUMED) with mission, instrument, resolution and assumptions. If a value is missing, the app says so; it never fills the gap with an estimate. If a limit cannot be fully evaluated, the verdict drops to CAUTION and says why.

- Limits are explicit: the values chosen by the team (e.g. 10 minutes without contact, 0.5 mSv per walk) are labeled as assumptions, and the user can adjust them (except the maximum slope); the verdict then says it used custom settings.

- Adding a new Mars site means adding one JSON file.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

The user is someone in a suit, in a hurry, with gloves and little bandwidth: high-contrast UI, nothing critical shown by color alone, and a printable strip of the route. We did not model dust storms, suit stiffness or the astronaut's physical state, and we say so rather than inventing an effect. It is an educational prototype, not flight software, and the app says so on screen.

TOOLS

Python (GDAL, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, SpiceyPy), FastAPI, React 19, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Three.js, Tailwind CSS, Zod, Zustand, Vite, nginx, AWS EC2 and S3, GitHub Actions, Linear.
